subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to rise on a question of privilege arising out of the tabling last evening by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) of a letter from Frank McMahon dated April 4, 1956. My question of privilege has to do with the fact that commencing on April 13 the Minister of Trade and Commerce denied in this house the possession of any documents from Frank McMahon. At no time did the minister raise the question that he had documents or that the documents were privileged; he denied that there were any such documents in his possession.
The first reference is to be found in Hansard of April 13, at page 2895, and the question asked is as follows:

subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce and ask him whether he would place before the house the offer reported to have been made by Gairdner and Company Limited as an alternative to the trans-Canada pipe line proposition now before the house? Would the minister also table any offer received from the company, and also the one from the McMahon interests relative to this matter?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext:
I shall be glad to table any documents I have. I have two documents from Gairdner and Company which I shall table; I have no documents from the McMahon interests.
And then on April 16 at page 2940 there was a motion-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: Order. May I interrupt the hon. member for Prince Albert to clarify one point. Have the documents he is now referring to been tabled as the result of a motion or have they been tabled voluntarily?

subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext:
The motion was for production and Your Honour will see at page 2940 the motion was for the production-
-of all letters and other documents received by the government or any minister or official from Mr. Frank McMahon or his agent or representative, and from Gairdner and Company Limited, since March 1, 1956, in which plans or offers have been made or suggested regarding the construction of a gas pipe line from Alberta to eastern Canada.
Then the minister said that he had filed the documents and my next remark was:
The McMahon documents were not filed.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext:
There were no
McMahon documents.
Again I point out that there was no question raised by the minister that he had in his possession any document that was confidential because it was so marked. He said that he had no document. Then at page 3258 of Hansard of April 25 there was a motion by myself as follows:
For a copy of any memoranda taken or made since March 25, 1956, by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys, or any official of either of their departments, or by anyone on their respective behalf, of any discussion or discussions with Mr. Frank McMahon, connected with or relative to any offer by him and his associates to build or construct a gas pipe line between the Alberta-Saskatchewan boundary and eastern Canada.
The minister took strong objection to having to keep a record of telephone conversations, and following that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) had this to say:
Mr. Speaker, before the question is put and since there is a Hansard record it might be well to point out that there is no mention here of telephone conversations.
The motion was put to the house and was defeated. Here is my question of privilege. I am not concerned and it is not any concern of the House of Commons as to whether the Minister of Trade and Commerce on his own received an alternative offer to the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines offer and concealed it from his colleagues, as apparently he did because the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said yesterday he had never heard of this.
As far as parliament is concerned my submission is that the answers given, to say the least, indicate that no reliance was placed on the fact, as was raised the day before yesterday for the first time, that the letters from McMahon were private and confidential. The answers given by the minister constituted a cavalier and flagrant contempt of parliament and certainly we are entitled to have the information we asked for unless the minister is able to say, "I cannot produce these because of their confidentiality." He said that there were no documents. That statement was completely incorrect. I ask the minister through you, sir, to explain why it was that this alternative offer, which until the day before yesterday he said he had never

Pipe Lines
received, as there were no documents, was not produced to parliament and why he persisted in his stand that at no time had he received any letter. Yet on April 4 he had received a letter setting out in detail an offer and criticizing as well the Trans-Canada proposition.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and' Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the question is: When is an offer an offer? An offer is not made to me personally as I am not building the pipe line. I am interested in having the government build the pipe line. The letter was marked "Private" and when a letter is marked in that way, if you are going to respect a document at all it must be private to you.

subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: Why did not you say that?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext:
Why did not I say
that? I get letters from my sister. I suppose I should announce in parliament when I receive a personal letter from my sister.

subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: About the pipe line?

subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: Is she advising you in regard to the pipe line?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: When a letter is marked "confidential" I believe it is supposed to be confidential. I may be wrong, and I notice that my hon. friends doubt that such things have any significance at all, but to me they do have. I have never double-crossed anybody in my life knowingly. Therefore I respect a private and confidential letter and I keep it private and I keep it confidential.

subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: Why did you not tell parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext:
That is a fine way to keep a letter private and confidential, to tell parliament about it. The front bench of the Conservative party amazes me.
Their idea of morality is most extraordinary. Just because another Conservative horse will not run, they are trying to say that I should disclose a private and confidential letter.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: The statement just made in no way deals with the point that was raised. That was the positive statement by the minister that there were no documents. If anybody was double-crossed, parliament was double-crossed by the minister.

subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext:
I
should like to draw the attention of the house to the fact that the confidential nature changed between early in April and May 2. On May 2 the minister said:
I have received no letter that I am free to table in this house.

That was a correct statement. That preserves the confidentiality, but why on May 2 he should tell us this and why he could not tell us earlier in the month is something nobody could possibly explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: I call your attention to the fact that a letter addressed to me that I am not free to table is not a document for parliament. I was asked for documents.

subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: Why didn't you tell the Prime Minister?

subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: Are we to understand that this answer is based on the theory that a letter is not a document? Is that the view we are now asked to accept?

subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: Order. May I state-

subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: I would-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: Order. I think the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has overlooked the fact that I was standing and asking for order. We have not yet embarked upon our routine proceedings. The hon. member for Prince Albert has raised a question of privilege. It was one between himself and the minister. The minister has given his explanation. I think now we ought to proceed with the routine proceedings.

subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: Your Honour, my question had to do with the minister's explanation.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: Does the hon. member contend that a question of privilege is one that facilitates a debate? Is a question of privilege debatable?

subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: No.

subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: I was proposing to ask-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: The answer is no. Let us go into routine proceedings.

subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: I was preparing to ask the minister to clarify the statement he has just made-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: He has given the answer to a question of privilege that was raised by the hon. member for Prince Albert.

subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: I rise on a point of privilege, Mr. Speaker. As a member of this house, I want to question your statement that the matter raised by the hon. member for Prince Albert concerned only him and the Minister of Trade and Commerce. As a member of this house I maintain that it concerns me when the question is the correctness of a minister's answer.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext:
I am sorry if I have aroused the indignation of the hon. member and perhaps of others. The word "procedure" comes from the Latin word "procedere", which means "go forward". I am here to keep things going. The point of privilege was raised by the hon. member for Prince Albert. He was listened to in silence, and I include myself among those who listened to him very reverently. The Minister of Trade and Commerce, in accordance with our rules, gave an explanation regarding the point of privilege which the hon. member for Prince Albert had raised. Hon. members have heard his answer. The debate that was pursued after that by the Leader of the Opposition and by the hon. member for Greenwood had to do with whether or not a document which is marked private is to be considered a document as far as this house is concerned. It is obvious that the Minister of Trade and Commerce held the view that a document marked private or confidential is not a document in the sense of documents that this house may require. To me this is absolutely right because at page 258 of May, fifteenth edition, I find the following:
However ample the power of each house to enforce the production of papers may be, a sufficient cause must be shown for the exercise of that power; and if considerations of public policy can be urged against a motion for papers, it is either withdrawn, or otherwise dealt with according to the judgment of the house.
I read this because it shows that there are documents that this house, however ample its power may be, is not entitled to have. How long am I going to allow a debate to go on? Even if the hon. member for Nanaimo is interested as I may be in having a debate on the question as to what is a document as far as this house is concerned, we are dealing here with what constitutes a private or confidential document and we could go on all day with such a debate. But we have an order paper and a question of privilege is not debatable. If the hon member can show me a reference indicating that a question of privilege is debatable I should like to see it.

subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: It can still be made.

subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, what was before Your Honour was not a debate.

subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: Oh, no!

subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: What was before Your Honour was very clear evidence of the fact that a misstatement had been made to this house.

subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: Order.

subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext:
That was what was being placed before Your Honour.
Pipe Lines

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: The Leader of the Opposition has his own view as to what was placed before him or what was placed before me. I suppose the Minister of Trade and Commerce also has his own view and I have mine. As far as I am concerned, I take it that a question of privilege was raised and an explanation was made by the person concerned. I have allowed a few questions because I felt that the house was prepared to have a few questions asked, but I think that now the house is willing to go ahead with the order of procedure.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I ask leave, under standing order 26 to move, seconded by the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker), the adjournment of the house for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely, the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce to the effect that there were no documents in the possession of the government from Frank McMahon, which was contrary to the fact, and the extent to which such incorrect statement made by the minister misled the house as well as his colleagues in the government with regard to the existence of a possible alternative pipe-line proposal for carrying gas from Alberta to eastern Canada.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Would the Leader of the Opposition, anyone in his party, or anyone in the house be kind enough to give me the reference in the authorities whereby a matter raised as a question of privilege can be the subject of a debate under standing order 26 instead of being pursued as a question of privilege in accordance with the procedure laid down for that type of matter? When a question of privilege is raised it may be the subject of a motion. It is then treated as such and takes precedence over all other matters, even motions by virtue of standing

Pipe Lines
order 26. It seems to me that if the hon. member for Prince Albert was not satisfied with the explanation given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce it was up to him to make a. motion immediately which was one of privilege. The hon. member does not recall that such incidents have taken place in the house?

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Your Honour stated that no debate was allowed and I adhered to your ruling and took my seat. No discussion was permitted.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: The hon. member knows that no debate can take place except, of course, if a motion is placed before the house. I have noted that in the last few years members who have raised questions of privilege have never pursued their points far enough in order to make them debatable. Once a question of privilege is raised it may be ended by a motion. Such motion may not be taken up immediately but a day may be appointed when it will be taken up. That, to me, should have been the course followed.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is not by way of continuance of a question of privilege. The statement was made by the hon. member on a question of privilege with regard to an answer he had received on different occasions. I am now raising this as a matter of procedure in this house, the position of the government in relation to parliament and the responsibility of ministers to answer correctly when questions are asked. I am putting forward a motion on that basis as a matter of urgent public importance in view of the fact that it has been announced that we may be debating the whole question of this pipe-line problem within a matter of a few days. I therefore submit, Mr. Speaker, that this is a motion correctly before the house at this time and that it is urgent because it is the one opportunity that will present itself for debate to determine whether or not there are other undisclosed offers which we have not been told about and which would provide us with a means of obtaining information that we should have before we proceed with a debate on this extremely important subject.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
If the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) himself were the subject of this motion, I am sure that he would have the right to insist upon having the house decide whether or not he himself had made a statement which was not correct. This motion, if it were allowed, would be debated all day and what would be the effect of it? At six o'clock tonight the house adjourns. The motion is predicated on the

assumption that the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) to the effect that there were no documents is incorrect. There is a point in dispute there. The minister says there were no documents that he could table. That was the sense of his explanation a moment ago but he said that there was a document or that there were documents marked private and confidential. Whether there was one document or more than one I do not know.
Arising out of that discussion that took place on the question of privilege, I think the matter should be the subject of a motion arising out of privilege and should be treated as such. I think that the one who is accused of a misstatement is entitled either to have that accusation confirmed by the house or to have his own stand that there was no misstatement vindicated by the house. As the matter stands now, this motion provides only for a debate but no chance for the house to express its views as to whether or not the statement made by the minister was a misstatement. I ask hon. members-any one of them

whether it is not true that if they were the subject of a motion of this kind, they would put forward the point that they are entitled to have their stand either condemned or vindicated by the house. By this motion such a thing could not take place. It is merely a motion to adjourn.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I say a word on the point of order that you have raised. In the first place, you suggested that a motion related directly to the question of privilege could be placed upon the order paper and a day appointed for debate. May I remind you-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: No, no.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Wrong again.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
What happens is this. I admit that it has been a long time since a question of privilege was pursued to its ultimate end. Perhaps it would be nice to have one again so that we would establish the procedure and everyone would know it and then the matter would not be so difficult. As the matter stands, many perhaps will say that I am laying down a new procedure that they have never heard of. However, it is there in the book. I do not bring my black notebooks into the house with me any more but later on I can get them and I will show hon. members precedents to the effect that when a question of privilege is raised, the member who is supposed to be concerned in it is entitled to explain. That is his right. Then the hon. member who raised the question may pursue the matter with a motion. He

makes a motion. That motion normally should be taken up immediately, be dealt with and decided upon; or someone may suggest, "We will take this up tomorrow". But these motions are not on the notice paper. They take place without notice. I would correct the hon. member when he says that you place a motion on the order paper. A motion with regard to privilege is one that must be taken up immediately.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I was only taking up your own expression in saying what I did on that point, because I understood you were saying that if a motion directly arising out of a question of privilege were put forward a day would be appointed for it. I only point out that if that were the position it would not be possible to get any such motion on now and have it introduced by a private member unless the government undertook to sponsor it.
Now, you commenced your remarks this morning on this point of order by asking hon. members to point out to you where the procedure under standing order No. 26 had been used in relation to a matter that had been the subject of a question of privilege. With respect, Mr. Speaker, I should like to put before you this view that it is quite erroneous to assume that the procedure offered by standing order No. 26 cannot be used for this purpose. Why should it not be? I speak subject to correction, but I am not aware of any occasion upon which there has been a positive ruling that the procedure under standing order No. 26 cannot be used in relation to a motion of this kind. Therefore, I say to you I think it is quite erroneous to assume, in the absence of any such decision, that this procedure under standing order No. 26 is not available in cases of this kind.
I ask you further to consider this point, Mr. Speaker. You say this is simply a question of privilege. It certainly arises out of what has been said this morning in relation to the question of privilege, but here is a matter that has implications in it that go beyond what has passed back and forth this morning, having been uttered on one part on the question of privilege and on the other part by the minister in attempting an explanation. This motion introduced by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) is a motion that goes right to the vitals of our parliamentary system. It is for that reason it is a matter of urgent public importance. Holding the views we do, nothing could be of greater public importance. In the situation which exists within the context in which this motion is brought forward, and in the context of the question of privilege brought forward today, nothing could be more urgent.
Pipe Lines
Therefore I am submitting to you, on the point of order on which you are proceeding now to base a ruling on the motion, that it is a very proper motion under the procedure available here under standing order No. 26 and that there is no other available procedure to deal with this situation.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I was very glad to hear the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) speak about procedure so enthusiastically and with great warmth. Evidently he likes procedure as much as I do, so I shall put him in my club.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Do not put your club on me.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
No, that would be a different club. It has been a long time since the club of the Speaker was ornamented and put on the table where it has become known as the mace.
Has the hon. member looked at standing order 26, subsection 6, paragraph (e):
The right to move the adjournment of the house for the above purposes is subject to the following restrictions:
(e) The motion must not raise a question of privilege.
That is where the whole issue lies between hon. members and myself. It is a question of privilege. I think the hon. member so indicated a moment ago when he said that this matter was so important it went deep down into the roots of our parliamentary system. That is my reason for not accepting the amendment.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: May I make my point clearer. You say you are proposing to regard this as a motion raising a question of privilege. My point was that it is not just a question of privilege. It is true it arises out of a discussion here this morning that began with a question of privilege, but it is something that goes far beyond any question of privilege.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
It may go far beyond, but there is in it a question of privilege. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), in that motion which is one for the adjournment of the house, is accused of having made a misstatement. If the hon. member for Eglinton were accused, as the minister is, and if someone were to ask me that this matter be made one of privilege and a motion were brought by which he could either be condemned or vindicated by the house, I would say by all means let us have the motion. This motion under standing order 26 may be debated all day until the adjournment at six o'clock.
What is the position with respect to the accusation against the minister? So far as the house is concerned, when we adjourn at

Pipe Lines
six o'clock, there will still be the accusation that he made a misstatement. The minister is entitled to have the house decide on the statement made by the hon. member for Prince Albert or concerning any other speeches accusing him of a misstatement, and on his own explanation and any other speeches made on his behalf taking his point of view, to have the house decide whether or not he has made a misstatement.
There is a point at issue here; you are raising a question of privilege and to do so you say, "Let us move the adjournment of the house," and the result of the debate will be that we adjourn the house at six o'clock and the accusation still confronts the minister. The same thing would obtain if the hon. member or indeed if any other hon. member were concerned. It is a question of privilege and you have to deal with it as such.
The hon. member for Prince Albert should have pursued his point by moving a motion which might have been in the sense of this motion here. It would perhaps have been taken up immediately. Now we are into the routine proceedings and we must carry on.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: May I have one final word, Mr. Speaker? You heard this morning, Mr. Speaker, a question of privilege raised by the hon. member for Prince Albert. You heard the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in attempted explanation. And then when other hon. members sought to have something to say or sought to ask questions you ruled that the question of privilege had been disposed of and was not a debatable matter. I now submit to you that the question of privilege was then disposed of-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I would be very happy to assist hon. members if they were to consult me before they made a move but While they are making a point in the house I cannot very well leave the throne and go and tell them what to do. They were not moving a motion; they were just debating. No matter how many hon. members think it was their question, the fact remains that the question of privilege was raised by the hon. member for Prince Albert, and it was up to him to move a motion. It was up to him to continue this matter to its proper conclusion. But I say that by virtue of section 26, 6 (e) and also because of the fact that this matter -a serious matter amounting to an accusation that the minister misinformed the house -is one of those matters which you cannot raise, save upon a substantive motion, an adjournment motion under standing order 26 cannot be accepted.

Hon. members know the story of this. I am sorry that we have spent so much time because of a point of procedure and it is now 20 minutes to 12. I do not like to have to talk about procedure any more than is necessary but hon. members remember the story of this kind of appeal.
Mr. Speaker Black was the first one who made the ruling that there was no appeal of his decisions that motions should not be accepted because he was given the discretion under the old standing order No. 31, now standing order 26, to decide whether or not in his view a motion should be accepted.
Mr. Ralston, who was then an hon. member of the opposition, appealed the Speaker's ruling that there was no appeal. Mr. Speaker Black on other similar decisions later on ruled in the same way and no appeal was made of his ruling. The matter was tried again in Mr. Speaker Fauteux's time and again in my time. When I made the ruling that there was no appeal the Leader of the Opposition made a similar appeal basing his action on the action of Mr. Ralston in 1932.
Hon. members will recall that at that time I said as far as I am concerned there will be no further appeal of my rulings that there is no appeal on this standing order.
Although I was perhaps convinced at the beginning of my term that hon. members would want to support the Chair with respect to this rule that rulings are not debatable, I have tried-hon. members know that-but I have come to the conclusion that it is almost an illusion for any Speaker to think that when he makes his rulings the rulings are not debatable, because hon. members choose to debate them.
Pipe Lines
The authority of the Canadian Speaker is such that it is entirely in the hands of the house. Notwithstanding what I said at that time, if I were to say here that there is no appeal of my ruling some hon. members might say, "Well, he is being autocratic; he does not want to have his rulings appealed", so I have taken the view, because I feel it is the wish of the house to keep the Speaker in their hands and to have that sort of check on him, that they want to have an appeal so I did not make any objection. As a matter of fact I offered an hon. member an opportunity to appeal my ruling not very long ago. That is my position now. It is true that there are more decisions sustaining the Speaker's ruling that there is no appeal of his decision under standing order 26 than that his decision is appealable. It is true that the weight of opinion is on that side. I might clear the position by allowing the house to decide. If there is another decision by the house sustaining the ruling I made last time it will give more weight to the position that there is no appeal from the Speaker's ruling, according to this standing order 26, when he decides that there is no appeal.

Mr. Speaker ruled that the statement was not in order and that the matter was not one of urgent public importance and moreover that there was no appeal from his decision.

speechtext:
I just want to finalize the statement I made when the matter was raised the last time. There is a distinction. I am very much impressed by the attitude taken by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. Standing order 26 reads:
(1)	Leave to make a motion for the adjournment of the house when made for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance-
(2)	The member desiring to make such a motion rises in his place, asks leave to move the adjournment of the house for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, and states the matter . . .
(3)	He then hands a written statement of the matter proposed to be discussed to Mr. Speaker, who, if he thinks it in order-
These are the words:
-and of urgent public importance-

By that standing order the Speaker has been given the discretion to decide whether it is in order and of urgent public importance. If in his view it is not in order or of urgent public importance he does not accept it. In 1932 Mr. Speaker Black, on a point of order raised by Mr. Ralston, gave a decision which appears at page 748 of Beauchesne's third edition, and I quote:
Mr. Speaker ruled that the statement was not in order and that the matter was not one of urgent public importance and moreover that there was no appeal from his decision.
Mr. Ralston appealed from the Speaker's refusal to permit an appeal from his decision.
I think there are three rulings to the effect that an appeal can take place, and if I recall correctly there are four or five to the contrary. On page 855 of the Journals for Tuesday, July 5, 1955, I find this:
Now, there were several occasions when standing order 31 was moved.
That is now standing order 26.
And the Leader of the Opposition will find that only on one other occasion, when Mr. Speaker Fauteux was Speaker, an appeal in similar circumstances to a decision of the Speaker that there was no appeal was granted. On all other occasions the house has always accepted the decision made by the Speaker, and also has always accepted the view that in those circumstances there was no appeal from the Speaker's ruling.
Of course I must decide on the spur of the moment, but if I had time I could give the exact references for the rulings. I quote from page 858 of the Journals of the same year:
In the future, whenever I make a ruling to the effect that the motion should not be accepted because it is not in order or is not of urgent public importance-that is that there is no urgency of debate-I will not grant an appeal from my decision that there is no appeal.
At that time the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar sustained the ruling I made, and so did the hon. member for Peace River. I should like very much to have this decided because I feel convinced that this is the right one. There are many people who seem to be interested in what is said from this chair, perhaps sometimes not for purely academic reasons, and I do not want any accusation made that I have not allowed an appeal although standing order 12 provides an appeal. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar will say, "If you are convinced you are doing the wrong thing, why do you do it?" After what he has said and after what the hon. member for Peace River has said and after I have had a chance to indicate why I had a moment of weakness, I shall stick to my guns and rule that there is no appeal.

subtopic: SEIZURE OF CANADIAN VESSELS ON LAKE ERIE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: SEIZURE OF CANADIAN VESSELS ON LAKE ERIE
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Fisheries. Can the minister give the house any information regarding the seizure of certain Canadian fishing vessels on lake Erie which I understand from a radio broadcast involved some shooting?

subtopic: SEIZURE OF CANADIAN VESSELS ON LAKE ERIE
speechtext:
My department has had no direct word on the matter because the administration of fisheries in Ontario is under the jurisdiction of the provincial government. However, this type of arrest is quite common on both coasts where fishermen, by accident or by design, cross the boundary line in territorial waters into the other nation's fishing grounds. The usual procedure is for the fisherman to come before the court of the country and have his case heard.
As far as shooting is concerned, all our Canadian patrol boats carry a gun in the bow and occasionally fire a shot by way of a warning across the bow of a fishing vessel they intend to arrest. I understand that was the nature of the shot fired in this case.

speechtext: We have reached resolution No. 390. Hon. members will And this vote on page 64 of the blue book of estimates and the details on page 492.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I believe I can probably comment on this item about the purchase of a site in the city of Guelph. I understand the government has decided that we need further accommodation for the federal building in Guelph and that plans were made to enlarge the post office building. This would mean that the officials of the customs branch, the Department of Veterans Affairs and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation would be congregated in the present post office or the new addition.
At the rear of the post office there is a considerable parking lot on which, during the seasons when the mail is not too heavy, some 30 to 40 automobiles of the employees are parked. Should there be an extension to the present building making use of the parking lot it would result in great inconvenience to people who shop in the city of Guelph. I should like to take this opportunity to convey to the minister the appreciation of the mayor, the board of trade, the planning commission and the parking authority for having his officials go to Guelph to meet the officials of the city and discuss the problem that would arise if it were decided to extend the present post office. They appreciated very much the opportunity of explaining to the minister's officials that they are planning to spend some $165,000 in the city of Guelph to remove existing buildings very close to the government parking lot in order to create a parking

area. They have asked me to thank the minister for meeting with them and for arriving at a decision which has given them reasonable assurance that the parking space will not be used for a building site. When the new federal building is built I hope that a suitable location will be found which will be satisfactory for the job the building has to do.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: I want to follow the suggestion made by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings on the last occasion these estimates were before the committee. I had hoped that the Prime Minister would be here but I realize that he cannot be here on all occasions. However, this is one matter during the discussion of which I should have liked to see him present.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: I will tell him about it.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: You are out of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: Order. Surely this discussion would not come under this particular item of the estimates of the Department of Public Works.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I stayed around here the other day and it came up under this item. I hope that I am not transgressing. I waited here for three hours for a chance to deal with this matter and I walked out momentarily. This is a matter that affects all the lawyers within our country and is one that I think deserves to be discussed. But, Mr. Chairman, if you say that it cannot be discussed, that is final. However, I point out that I was here the other day and that the matter came up only at ten minutes to six. I am asking the consideration of the committee in order that I may deal with it for a few minutes.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I would think the hon. member would have to have the unanimous consent of the committee because this discussion is clearly out of order on this item.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext:
Has the hon. member
unanimous consent to deal with this matter?

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: Agreed.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to point out that two or three other members wanted to revert to preceding items in the previous discussion of these estimates and

unanimous consent was not given to them. On the basis of fairness, I object to unanimous consent being given.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: So do I.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I disagree with the hon. member's statement. I have been here during every minute of the discussion of the estimates and my recollection is that two hon. members reverted to certain questions and it was agreed that they should do so. No one was refused.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: What items were they?

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: The minister has not his officials before him but I wonder whether he could give me any information as to what progress is being made on the advance planning of a new post office building in North Battleford and whether there is any possibility of a start being made on the building this year? maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: All I can say, Mr. Chairman, -and all I could say if the officials were here-is that the matter is in the planning stage. Until we get votes of parliament I am not in a position to go farther than that. This is a planning vote and that is one of the projects we have in the planning stage.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, are we on item 390?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: We are on item 390.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext:
Then I ask you to look at the wording of item 390 which is as follows:
To provide for advance planning of projects including acquisition of sites.
If the question of where the supreme court building should be placed in advance planning does not come within that item, then I am very much surprised.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: There is a supreme court building now.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: I raise this question, Mr. Chairman. If you hold against me, then I ask the usual consideration.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext:
I am, of course, in some difficulty in that I have before me a resolution in the following terms: Resolved that a sum not exceeding $1,500,000, less amounts voted in interim supply, be granted to Her Majesty for public works, general, to provide for advance planning of projects including acquisition of sites. In the details in the blue book at page 492 there is little, if any, additional information. The minister has indicated that an expenditure for the supreme
Supply-Public Works
court building is not included in this vote. I therefore do not see how the hon. member for Prince Albert could discuss that matter under this vote. I presume that there were other occasions on which the matter could have been discussed. For instance, I am quite certain that it could have been discussed, perhaps, under the first item of the departmental estimates. I regret very much if, by reason of our rules, the hon. member is prevented from discussing this question at this time. For that reason I transmitted to the committee a request for unanimous consent, but that consent was refused. I therefore feel that my hands are tied.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: I should like to ask a question of the minister under this item which is to provide for advance planning of projects including acquisition of sites. maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: No; not under the estimates of this department. Planning for a project of that nature, if it is to be done, would more appropriately come under the jurisdiction of my colleague who is responsible for the administration of national parks. We have done no planning under this vote.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: If further discussions take place with regard to the consideration of a civic centre and if as a result the Department of Public Works will be required to go ahead and carry out the construction, may I ask whether the Minister of Public Works would be advised before the final decision is made, so that he could use his good judgment in making decisions?

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: I presume so, Mr. Chairman; yes.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext:
You say you
presume so. I think the matter is of a little bit more importance than that. I think it is of sufficient importance that the minister should not just pass on a presumption on it. Maybe the minister can assure the committee that that would be so.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext:
No; I cannot do that. That matter is within the jurisdiction of my colleague. If he wants my advice, I should be glad to give it to him. But it is perfectly and entirely within his competence to make a decision if he chooses to do so.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: I have one question that I should like to ask the minister. It is not in connection with the national parks, so I am sure he will be able to answer it without referring it to another minister. The city of Medicine Hat has grown so much within the last eight years that the public building we have there-I refer to the post office-is entirely inadequate to handle the mail situation today. I am wondering whether the minister has given consideration to the acquisition of a new site for the post office and just what is being done in advance planning for a project of that kind.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: Order. The hon. member for Medicine Hat will recall that I interrupted another hon. member a few moments ago. Under these specific votes, I feel that we must deal with specific matters. Although this particular item reads, "to provide for advance planning", I do not think it opens to the members of the committee the opportunity to discuss their particular pet projects in all parts of Canada. If that were the case, it would lead to a debate which would be far more extensive than should take place under an item of this kind. Under this item, I really feel that we should deal with the particular subjects covered. I would ask the hon. member if he would co-operate with me in that respect.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext:
May I ask you
to define what is meant by advance planning of projects including the acquisition of sites? Now, certainly, advance planning-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: Order. It is, of course, not for me to interpret or try to interpret these votes in advance. But I might perhaps suggest this to the hon. member, that it is within his competence to ask the minister what is covered by this vote.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: Perhaps I could have brought up this question under item 360. However, there was no provision made for a post office in Medicine Hat, and I feel that some consideration should be given to a building there. I think that calls for advance planning. What I want to know now is whether or not the Minister of Public Works or the government is giving consideration to a building in Medicine Hat. I consider that advance planning, and I think that is what the item is for.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext:
I will be glad to keep in mind what the hon. member has said. This vote, as hon. members will recall, was introduced into the Department of Public Works about three years ago when I became responsible for this department. Formerly we could not consider the preparation of plans or the acquisition of sites unless we
[Mr. Winters.)

had a specific item in the estimates, and that meant that each year we carried over sums of money that we were not able to spend, and we had revote after revote. We, therefore, asked parliament to give us an amount of money, which in this case is a million and a half dollars, to enable us to do some preliminary planning and incur some expenditures against planning and acquiring sites, so that when we did get to the stage of coming forward with a project and putting an item in the estimates we would be in a better position to spend it. It seemed to me this was an opportunity to do some orderly planning.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: Can the minister tell us any sites he has in view at the present time?

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: No, I cannot say that.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: That was my point; in the city of Medicine Hat we have to have a new site and a new public building, and I was wondering what was being done by the minister in that respect. It was for that reason I asked the minister the question, which I think is a fair one under item 390.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: I have no wish, of course, to limit debate but hon. members will realize that if, under wording such as we find in this item, hon. members had the privilege of mentioning a project or several projects in every riding in Canada, we would arrive at an impossible result. It seems to me that these general remarks, and remarks to the effect that members are disappointed that a particular project is not proceeding, are the type of remarks that might be made on the first item in connection with policy. I think most hon. members agree that would contribute to more orderly debate.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, now that we have this item I may say that I am opposed to these general items unless we have particulars. I wanted to deal with the subject of planning and expenditure in connection with a parking space and the destruction of the old supreme court. Now that the minister has blocked it we shall start to try to find out where these projects are.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: On a question of privilege; the minister did not block it, the committee blocked it.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: Oh, yes he did. We will get along well if that is the minister's attitude.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: Let us have a clear understanding on this. Is the hon. member threatening us or doing something of that nature?

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: I am just saying we are going to get information for a change.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: If we are going to be threatened and bulldozed, parliament is not going to do the business of the country very well.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: It is hard to get information from ministers.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: Not from me.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: Where is the million and a half going to be spent? What are the projects in mind? Handing the minister a million and a half to play around with, without anything to justify it-

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: Well, express your views. You have had two years to do it. This is the third year this item has been in the estimates.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: Let us have the particulars, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: Before too much heat is generated, may I suggest to the hon. member that he should address the chair rather than speak directly across the chamber to the minister. I am sure we would have a more orderly debate.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: The minister should let us hear about some of these projects that he has in mind for the million and a half dollars. There was no objection raised, Mr. Chairman, when the hon. member for Wellington South dealt with one of these projects. What are these projects the minister has in mind? Has he made any projections of them? Let us have some of the particulars as to how this is to be made up and why the amount has been fixed at one and a half million?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: Pursuing the particular point and pursuing the same desire to get information, can the minister tell us how last year's vote was spent? According to the details, $317,452 was actually spent up to December 1, 1955; surely he could tell us how that money was spent. Then, he will note that the estimated amount for the balance of the year was $932,548. I realize that at the time the blue-book was printed that money had not been spent, but could he tell us now whether that $932,548 was spent in whole or in part and how it was spent? He could tell us, in the usual forthright manner in which he likes to hand out information, how this money was spent last year and then that would give us some guide as to the kind of expenditure this money is for and perhaps then we could get some intelligent answers to our questions as to what this year's vote is to be spent upon.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext:
I cannot, of course, tell what this year's vote will be spent upon because I do not know. I am asking parliament to
Supply-Public Works
vote a million and a half dollars to enable me to plan projects as they come up for consideration. If I were in a position to know exactly where it was going to be spent, I could put specific votes in the estimates and I would not need to ask for this pool arrangement. But it may be that a project will come forward in any community across Canada upon which we would like to do some advance planning and perhaps acquire sites so that when the plans are prepared we will be ready to develop the structure.
I am not, therefore, in a position to detail what it is for, and the very nature of the vote indicates that it is planning as required. It has always met with the approval of parliament. As a matter of fact, I recall the first time it was put in the estimates it was rather welcomed as being a step in the direction of orderly estimating, and I think it has helped us to do that. If hon. members are in disagreement with that, then of course they are at liberty to express their views. I would be glad to get a breakdown of how the amount was spent last year.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: It was suggested a few moments ago by the previous chairman that it would be quite in order to ask the minister what projects he had in view or what sites. I asked him that question and he said he had not any sites in view. That being the case, surely it must be in order for members to suggest to the minister what projects might be carried out under this item.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: They are quite in order to suggest what they think should come under this item by way of planning and the acquisition of sites.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: The minister would not object to that.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: No.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: I do not want to take the minister off the hook, particularly, but we had a certain amount of work done in Bayfield last year for which there was no item in the estimates. I think that is perhaps where some of this money goes, is it not?

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: If it is a matter of planning and acquiring a site, if we acquired a site under that vote, then that is the case. It gives us the opportunity of doing this so we can deal more expeditiously with the actual carrying out of the work. I hope this commends itself to hon. members as a good approach to the matter of estimating and doing work, because I personally think it is.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext:
I think that the work that was done in Bayfield certainly was not in the estimates and it had to be paid out of the

Supply-Public Works
same fund. I just suggest to the minister that we have another project at Port Albert which needs some attention. The project is at the mouth of the natural harbour at Port Albert which is a fine place for boats to slip into out of the storms that often occur on lake Huron. All that is needed is a little dredging at the mouth of the river, at the natural harbour there. At the present time I do not think boats can get in and out of there because of a sandbar.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext:
May I ask the minister if this vote merely covers the planning of design and the acquisition of land or whether it includes any form of economic planning? It seems to me that many decisions are made by this department based purely upon the engineering requirements or the engineering benefits whereas decisions frequently have to be made as between two suggested projects based very largely upon the economic value of those two places.
I would like to refer to an instance where I understand the department is carrying out an investigation which I presume comes under this amount. My example refers to the relative value of a structure in two points. I have raised the question and the boards of trade on the south coast of Vancouver island have asked for greater facilities in connection with harbours. The last report I had from the department was that they were investigating the advisability of constructing additional harbour facilities either at San Juan or at Sooke. It was not a question of both of these places being developed; it was a question of one or the other being developed. No doubt that is an investigation which is being carried out under this item.
I would like the minister to tell us how far he has progressed with that investigation. I would particularly like to know whether the economic side of these problems is investigated by his department under this item.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman, this item just covers the architectural or engineering planning, the actual preparation of plans and specifications on an advanced basis and the acquisition of sites.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: In a case such as I have raised, is the decision made as between the relative values of the two harbours or is it based solely upon the engineering advantages? Where is the economic side discussed? Has the department any economics branch? Could the minister explain where that is covered?

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext:
We have a small economic branch in the department, Mr. Chairman,
[Mr. Cardiff.!
and the vote is through the general administrative item. These things are not determined solely on the basis of the engineering merits but are considered in the light of economic circumstances as well.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre asked how much of last year's vote was actually spent. The answer is that on building construction projects we spent $234,738.07; on engineering projects we spent $233,413.31, or a total of $468,151.38.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, on that same question, could the minister not give a greater breakdown than that?

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: Yes, how much do you want?

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: That is almost as good as the pipe line answers.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY

Mr. Chairman, I know the minister is anxious to utter the sigh of relief that will come when his estimates are completed and I wish to accommodate him by being very brief in my remarks. I cannot let this item go by without once again drawing the attention of the minister and his officials to the urgent need of buildings in Edmonton East, particularly in the town of Beverly in order to accommodate a post office. I believe that part of this appropriation would be justly spent for the acquisition of a site and the planning of such a project in that area. I do not know of any other place of comparable size or importance that has had as little public investment by the government as Edmonton, and particularly Edmonton East. It is true that a new federal building is being constructed which is coming along very nicely and we are grateful for that, but we should remember that this project has come about after some 15 years of making strong representations to get it.
On several occasions in the past I have endeavoured to draw the attention of the minister to the urgency for a public building in the town of Beverly and on each occasion I have not been very successful. At the present time the post office in that town is nothing more than a small wooden shack which is disgracefully inadequate. I would appreciate it very much if the minister and his officials would investigate the possibility of erecting a suitable public building in that town. I have communicated with the Post Office Department and they of course give the explanation that the decision has to be made by the Department of Public Works. The minister will probably answer me by saying that the recommendation has to come from the Post Office Department. It seems to me that is classic buckpassing and is not fair at all to the people in that region.
There is another point I wish to make. In the city of Edmonton real estate values are rising constantly. I think it would be good business and good economics for us to invest in sites and make plans in order to provide for the needs of the community. Recently I received a submission from the Edmonton businessmen's association which drew my attention to the fact that in Edmonton East particularly most of the post office services are located in grocery stores and other retail shops. In a country such as Canada I think
fMr. Hamilton (Notre Dame tie Grace).]
that also is disgraceful, especially in urban areas. All I ask at this time is that the minister assure me that he will investigate and examine the conditions there with a view to using some of this money in order to acquire sites for such projects.

That being so, some doubt arises as to the purpose of the item. In other sections of his estimates there are large items which are not specifically pinned down to one particular matter. I hope the minister is not going to get into the habit of the Department of National Defence and set up his estimates in the form of a revolving fund which will not be changed from year to year.
With regard to this particular item the minister said-he can correct me if I have made an incorrect note-in response to a question as to what would happen in the coming year with respect to the distribution of the $1,500,000 available, that he supposed that the division of the money would bear some relation to the population of the various provinces. May I point out that there was no such disposition of the money last year because, according to the figures that the minister read, the province of Manitoba seems to have been relegated to a position almost off his list. We were blacklisted, having an

expenditure of only $2,000 for public buildings and $315 for engineering. Can the minister inform us just what was done in Manitoba last year and why it was placed in such an inferior position compared with the rest of Canada? Second, in this planning activity and acquisition of sites what does the department do when it acquires sites that are not subsequently used for the original purpose for which they were procured? Some of the sites that the department obtains possession of are secured by means of expropriation of property; but if the site is not used for the purpose originally intended, is that expropriated property returned to the original owner? I put those two questions before the minister.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext:
I will answer those two questions, Mr. Chairman, and I will deal with the second one first, as to what we do with property if we expropriate it and then do not subsequently use it. That is something that happens very seldom, indeed, but it happened in one instance in Winnipeg. I am sure that is the instance that my hon. friend has in mind. We have declared the property to be surplus and have turned it over to Crown Assets Disposal Corporation. That crown company reports to the Minister of Trade and Commerce and it is his responsibility to dispose of the property. He has that matter in hand now.
With regard to the other question, namely as to why Manitoba was discriminated against, may I say I do not think there is any question of that. The results are the best answer. It is not how much planning we do that determines always what results will be obtained. It is the actual structures that are the pay-off, if I may use that word. I know he realizes that Manitoba has been far from discriminated against.

Some doubt has been raised as to the advisability of granting to the minister a blank cheque for $1,500,000 with which to do as he may deem necessary during the course of the coming year. However, I should like to point out that item 364 was of a similar nature and asked for $900,000. Item 389 was of a similar nature again, and asked for the sum of $800,000. We have item 390 which is now before us and which asks for $1,500,000. Item 391 is another
fMr. Pallett.]
similar item calling for $750,000 and item 392 calls for $650,000. That is a grand total of some $4,600,000. However, last year at the end of March in supplementary estimates he asked for an amount in excess of $4 million. I hope the minister can give a further reply in addition to what he gave me the other day with regard to why not more of these items could be left until the last week in March when the house has, I believe, always been most reasonable and, upon satisfactory explanation, has never yet failed to vote the money in emergency funds that he found it necessary to ask for at that time. In the United States the Hoover commission went very carefully over the items that had been budgeted for and that had been in the accounts for years. One thing that they found that was a dangerous item was an item such as this. It is an encouragement to overexpenditure. One million and a half dollars is given by parliament without strings attached, without even a suggestion by the minister as to why the additional quarter of a million dollars is needed, without even a general outline as to how it is going to be expended. This is the type of item that encourages departmental officials to spend, spend and spend.

Under this item, I should like to ask the minister whether he can say anything further with respect to the matter to which I drew his attention yesterday on the orders of the day. I asked him then whether he had yet seen the press report by Gerald Waring concerning the extent to which the chartered banks have reduced their lending for the construction of new homes. The minister indicated that he had not yet seen that report and he also suggested that, if the government had any thought of going more directly into the field of lending by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, that would be a matter of government policy, to be announced in due course.
It seems to me that a report such as that which Gerald Waring gave in his column, Which was published in a number of newspapers yesterday, does call for some comment by the minister. As I interpret this report, it seems that, as a result of the advice given by the Bank of Canada to the chartered banks to put certain brakes on credit, the banks have carried out that advice with respect to housing. I understand that the advice given by the Bank of Canada was
Supply-Public Works
that housing was the one field where credit should not be curtailed; yet Mr. Waring's report is that this is the very field in which it has happened. His report indicates that loans by the banks for new housing so far in 1956 are 30 per cent below what they were at the same time last year. In the light of that, it seems to me that the question I put to the minister yesterday is more than appropriate, when I asked him if the government would consider expanding its activities in the field of direct loans for housing construction.
It should be pointed out to the minister that the suggestion contained in my question of yesterday, the suggestion contained in Gerald Waring's report, could not have come as any surprise to the minister. Indeed, on January 18 of this year, my colleague, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, as recorded on page 249 of Hansard, asked the following question of the minister:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Public Works. In view of yesterday's announcement by the banks indicating a decline in money being available for housing, would the government consider again supplying a portion of N.H.A. funds as it did before the first session of this parliament?
The minister asked permission to take the question as notice. He answered it the next day in what we must take as a considered fashion, and this in part is what he said, as recorded on page 281 of Hansard:
There has been no indication by prospective borrowers that there is a general shortage of mortgage money under the National Housing Act. As the hon. member knows, the act contains authority by which Central Mortgage may make loans directly to borrowers if loans are not being made available by approved lenders. If a shortage of mortgage money did occur it would be a matter of government policy, in light of the circumstances at that time, to determine to what extent the corporation's power to make direct loans should be used. At the present time this authority is being used in the smaller communities. It is the government's intention to insure that a high leveL of house building continues.
That was the declared position of the minister on January 19, but we are now led to believe that there has been a considerable reduction in the lending of money by the banks for the construction of new homes. In the light of that, it seems to me that the time has come for the government to implement its indication, as set out on January 19, by expanding its activities in the field of direct loans for housing construction. I think it would be appropriate that the minister make some statement on this matter at this time.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext:
This is rather far afield when one relates it to the wording of the item but, since the hon. member did have the impression he could discuss some general

Supply-Public Works
items on housing, I shall comment. But at the same time I hope that we will not widen this discussion to a general debate on housing, particularly having in mind that we have just had two full-scale debates on housing, one on the resolution stage and the other on the second reading stage of the amendments to the National Housing Act. The situation, as the hon. member knows, is that money has tightened up and the flow of funds available for mortgages has tightened correspondingly. It was for that reason that we gave very serious consideration to this matter recently and took the step of raising the ceiling for mortgage money under the National Housing Act from 5J to 5J per cent, which restored it to the level at which it was established in 1954 when the act was amended to enable the chartered banks to make loans against the security of residential mortgages. That has stimulated a flow of mortgage money. It is still below last year's level.
But on the other hand we came into this present year with a carry-over of some 80,000 units under construction and to date starts have been above the level even of last year which was a record level in itself. A great deal of that is because of forward commitments by lenders but the fact is we are still getting a very high level of house building activity. What the future monetary trends will be it is hard to tell at this moment, but we are in the fortunate position of having a heavy carry-over coming into this year and having a high level of house building activity that has prevailed up to this time and shows healthy signs of continuing. Basically those are the factors that confront us now. As I have said, the government wishes to see a continuing high level of housing activity and we are studying the situation at all times, as my hon. friend can well imagine.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
