Housing starts have remained high on the strength of bank commitments made before credit was tightened. But housing officials expect the dollar downhold will show up markedly in a month or two, at a time of year when home construction normally would be approaching peak activity.
It seems to me that the time to face a crisis such as that is in advance rather than after it has come upon us. I wonder whether the Minister of Public Works has had a heart to heart discussion with his colleague, the Minister of Finance, about this matter. It

seems to me that it was a logical and commendable bit of advice to give the banks that in curtailing credit they should not apply the brakes on credit for the construction of homes. Banks are in business for the purpose of making money and one cannot blame them if they have a particular interest in their better customers, if we may call them that. But surely if advice is going to be given to the banks with respect to lending for home construction the government should pursue the matter and see that that advice is acted upon.
I am glad to note that the minister is studying the matter but I suggest that it requires pretty active consideration right now rather than after the slow-down has become evident, which in turn involves another delay before anything is done. May I ask one other question. Has the minister any comment to make on the rumour that the government might try to meet the situation by buying such mortgage paper as the banks hold so as to increase to that extent the credit they might have available for housing?

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: There is provision made for that operation under the statute now. I do not think I should comment beyond that on the government's intentions.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: Then can the minister indicate to the committee the extent to which direct loans by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for housing are in operation?

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext:
The policy is that direct loans by C.M.H.C. are made where the lending operations of other lending institutions are not the normal practice. As I said when discussing the amendments on second reading, two years ago before the banks came into the picture there was quite a high level of direct activity on the part of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, but the need for that has dropped because the 4,000 odd branches of the chartered banks have in effect been lending agencies in many communities that were not previously served by mortgage money under the National Housing Act. To date there has been no decided trend one way or the other in that feature of operations under the act.
But all these things are matters which we are studying and, as I said, the situation is that so far we have a high level of housing activity. We have been observing the trends and studying every feature of the situation. The hon. member advocates that we keep as close to it as we can. I can assure him that we are doing that.

Thank you very much for your consideration, Mr. Chairman. I was saying that for some time it has been of some concern to us that when we build homes for our senior citizens with the assistance of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, we do manage to obtain a grant from the provincial government towards the cost of these homes of roughly one-third. I am referring specifically now to such organizations as the Burnaby New Vista Society. A large share of the money had to be raised by voluntary effort and that, to some degree, may be desirable and wholesome.
However, I never was particularly proud of the role played by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, because their assistance consists only of a loan which has to be repaid. If the minister were able to persuade

his colleagues in the government to aid the cost of housing for our senior citizens, at least to the extent of the provincial aid in this respect, we would be able to reduce the rental to these people on low incomes by a considerable degree. By the time these 40 and 50 year mortgages are repaid, in effect we have repaid twice the amount borrowed. If there is any way, therefore, in which the minister could clear himself with his colleagues and use the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation not for the purpose of granting mortgages on these homes but for the purpose of making grants towards the construction of these homes, I think it would be greatly appreciated throughout the country.
The other little thing I intended to say was on the subject of the insurance that now prevails on all N.H.A. loans. I should like to see this insurance feature extended to include insurance for the borrower as well as for the lender. I feel that, in the first place, we should have thought of insurance for the borrower. However, the government in its wisdom at the time decided that the welfare of the lender was more important and therefore the insurance feature was introduced. Everyone buying a house under N.H.A. is forced now to pay an insurance premium so that if he cannot meet his payments the lender receives full protection. I feel that the minister could, with very little administrative difficulty, extend the insurance feature to provide insurance for the borrower. I am sure that by now the minister must be well aware of the fact that when homes are financed by life insurance companies an insurance salesman shows up at the door shortly after the family occupies the home. He does his utmost to persuade the family to buy term life insurance or mortgage insurance as it is sometimes called, so that if the head of the family passes away the balance of the mortgage will be paid. There are other catastrophes besides the death of the breadwinner of the family, and I think at very little inconvenience to his department this insurance feature could be introduced and the government would not then be on record as being only interested in the welfare of the lender but would also have shown some concern for the welfare of the borrower.
There is one other minor detail I wish to mention, although in Burnaby it is now a major detail, and that is the apparent arbitrary ruling that now applies to some of the suburban areas that no N.H.A. loan shall be granted where septic tanks are planned. Our municipal council back home has attempted to get Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to modify this policy somewhat and they
Supply-Public Works
are asking that where the municipal engineering department can prove that plans actually are in existence for the sewer, the loan under N.H.A. be approved. However, the departmental officials have not yet seen their way clear to grant what I consider to be a very modest request. We almost get back to the old conundrum of which came first, the chicken or the egg. Unless the prospective house builder knows that he will be able to get an N.H.A. loan he is unwilling to buy the subdivision or the set of lots offered for sale, yet Central Mortgage and Housing say that until the sewer is in we are unwilling to approve these lots. The minister well knows that councils in suburban areas are not in a position to instal sewers through undeveloped areas. Things have, therefore, reached a sort of stalemate and a problem has arisen that will have to be resolved. While I should like to see sewers along every alley in these suburban municipalities, I think the minister will agree it is a financial and physical impossibility. I think a bit more leniency mght be extended and some agreement reached with these municipalities whereby if they express willingness to instal sewers, if and when the subdivision takes place, then the N.H.A. financing will be made possible.
I should like to close with a reiteration of the statement the minister made to me on January 19 when he said it is the government's intention to ensure that a high level of housebuilding continue. Today he said something to the effect that what future concerns will be no one seems to know at the moment. I hope the minister will not lock the stable door after the horse has run away. I hope he will keep the situation well in mind and also keep the situation six months or a year from now well in mind. I think he will agree that bank lending has been greatly reduced and that it is the intention of the banks to hold their percentage of investment in housing at approximately the level that now exists. Other sources of mortgage money, therefore, will have to be found. I should like to seriously urge upon him that he ask his colleagues to again consider having the governments supply a portion of N.H.A. funds.

The veterans concerned, the city council of Trail, the legion and people generally in the district thought the price was too high. I made representations on their behalf and also suggested that, in view of this general dissatisfaction with the price established by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, there should be an impartial appraiser appointed to go into the situation.
The minister did not agree with that. In fact, in reply to my suggestion on the estimates, he wrote me on July 20 the following letter:
We are unable to accede to the request that an impartial appraiser be appointed for the purpose of establishing a sale value on the houses in question. We believe that a fair price has been established for the houses in Trail and that it is below the market value of comparable houses in the municipality. We therefore do not think any purpose would be served by following the proposal to which you refer.
In addition, during the debate the minister gave some figures to indicate how well these houses that were being put up for sale were selling generally across Canada. I do not think his figures referred to the Sunningdale project, because that has not been the fact in Sunningdale. As a matter of fact, according to information I received just a few days ggo, out of 175 houses put up for sale in the Sunningdale project to date, only seven have been sold. That is an indication of the attitude of the tenants and others generally toward the prices established for these houses.
What is the result? A great number of the veteran tenants, owing to the fact that they see little opportunity of purchasing houses at a reasonable figure, are vacating, going into other districts and building their own homes, which they claim they can do to better advantage. Those who are staying and the new tenants are definitely not taking the same care of the property; the maintenance is not being carried on as well, so the project as a whole is deteriorating at a much greater rate than it did prior to the government's announcement of the prices for the purchase of these houses.
It has been proven by experience that the minister's optimism in this respect was unjustified, with the sale of seven houses out of 175 in something under 12 months and the veterans concerned, or the majority of them, and those remaining there not maintaining the houses as well as formerly. In view of the attitude of the city council, of the Legion

of the area and of the veterans' committee representing the veteran tenants, it does justify a reappraisal of the situation to see if the minister's officials have unwisely advised him. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the problem to which my hon. friend has referred is an important and difficult one and is encountered by civil servants everywhere when comparison is made of their salaries and allowances with those of the more highly paid echelons of business and industry. I am sure my hon. friend is aware that a problem of this kind receives continuous study by the treasury board and the civil service commission; for those in the north who are affected very naturally and properly voice their sentiments in regard to this disparity to which my hon. friend refers.
The two governmental boards to which I have referred do the best they can to bridge the gap between the emoluments of civil servants, and members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police on the one hand and employees of private concerns, on the other. To balance completely the amounts paid to civil servants with the allowances paid by private industry and contractors to employees working in the northern sections of Canada, I do not think could be justified to the taxpayer.

I realize there is a problem, and it was that problem I raised. But how are you trying to effect a balance? What are the northern rates of pay and where are they applicable? I understand that an additional allowance is granted to R.C.M.P. personnel serving in certain parts of northern Canada.

speechtext:
The special northern subsistence allowance is $1.50 a day. The special northern allowance is $3 per day in some cases and $2 per day in others. The special northern subsistence allowance provides for $1.50 per day for Royal Canadian Mounted Police personnel serving in detachments which by their remoteness are designated as isolated. It is paid in lieu of meals or rations in kind.
The special northern allowance is as follows. The privy council recently approved

of an amendment to Royal Canadian Mounted Police regulations granting the commissioner authority to pay a cash allowance in lieu of rations to members of the force stationed at points within the Northwest Territories, the Yukon, that part of the province of Quebec lying north of the 55th parallel of latitude, and Labrador, at which it is convenient to purchase food. The cash allowance approved is $3 per diem for married members not in receipt of rations in kind, and $2 per diem for single members not in receipt of rations in kind.
Prior to the approval of the northern allowances, members of the force in the areas defined above and not in receipt of rations, received the special northern subsistence allowance of $1.50 per diem.
What was the date of that order in council? Was it this year, or ten years ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It was some months ago, not years ago. I can get the exact date for my hon. friend, but I do not have it at the moment. It was some months ago.
That would really be before the tremendous development that has taken place in the north?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, I would not say that.

If it was some months ago it might well have been before the development of the construction of the D.E.W. line, for instance, had taken place. However, let that be. I should like, if I may, to make this observation. I think the members of the force who are stationed in the north are certainly to be very highly commended for the standard of discipline and morale they have maintained in spite of the very wide difference in pay rates between the members of the force and the civilians working in that area. I feel that it is most commendable, and I suggest to the government that I hardly think the special allowances the minister has mentioned are adequate in view of present conditions.

I do not know why they are not entitled to the same consideration as civil servants in the northern part of our country. Single civil servants receive $900 and married civil servants $1,500 per year. I was wondering whether any consideration has been given to that problem.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I can certainly say without any question at all that very great consideration has been given to these matters, because they are considered by the treasury board and the civil service commission from time to time. But it is difficult to draw
Supply-Justice
comparisons under this heading without taking into account other circumstances of, say, civil servants in the north, in the matter of housing, for example, and practices in the departments concerned.
My information is that the allowances are not necessarily uniform as among other departments of the government, and there are reasons for that. In the case of Royal Canadian Mounted Police personnel, for example, they receive housing for which they pay a rent not greater than that in the more settled parts of Canada, in spite of the fact that, as my hon. friend from the Yukon knows, it costs the federal government a very great deal more to provide that housing.
In that respect the government would not be getting an economic rent for the investment that would be represented by that house, though it would be high enough for the member of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to pay in relation to his salary. The only way in which a balanced view can be obtained of any one of these items is to consider it in relation to them all, and that is rather a difficult comparison to make in the type of discussion we are carrying on this afternoon.

I notice that this item has increased by $1,205,000. I gather that, since the Minister of Finance announced the recent increases, it is necessary to make a further adjustment. I wonder whether in due course the minister could say how much the adjustment will be?
While I am on my feet I should like to say that the minister maintains very high standards for this service, and I think that is desirable; but I have a feeling the compensation provided for members of the R.C.M.P. is not adequate. I wonder whether the minister could give some comparison of prevailing rates paid in cities like Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver to their police forces, if he has that available.
I have known a number of men who have given a lifetime to the service. I am sure they did not enter the service with a view to making a fortune, but I think they should not be expected to remain in the position where they will have to worry the rest of their lives and try to qualify after retiring age for jobs that are not too easy to find. I wonder whether the minister could also make some comment upon the medieval custom, that has existed for too long a time, that men should be denied the rights of married life for extended periods.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Would my hon. friend permit me to reply to his first question. Then I would be very glad to deal with the question of marriage afterward.

Supply-Justice
On the floor of this house I do not like to make comparisons with, say, the Montreal police force or the Winnipeg police force or any of the other police forces in Canada. But I think the general statement can be made that the salaries of the members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police force compare very favourably with those of most of the police forces in Canada. It is very proper that they should, because in the selection of our personnel we maintain, upon the average, somewhat higher standards than those which prevail in many of these other police forces.
I have not the pay schedule of any of these other police forces here, but I have that of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police force. The present annual salary of a third-class constable is $2,436. The revised annual salary that went into effect with the last increases as of April 1 this year is $2,640. For second-class constable the rates are $2,760 and $3,000. For first-class constable the salary in effect
now is as follows:
First year	 $3,240
Second year	 3,420
Third year	 3,600
Fourth year	 3,780
Fifth year	'	 4,020
Then we have corporal, from $4,320 to $4,500; sergeant, from $4,740 to $4,980; staff sergeant, from $5,220 to $5,460; corps sergeant-major, $5,640; sub-inspector, $6,660; inspector, ranging from $6,960 to $7,620; superintendent, from $7,920 to $8,580; assistant commissioner, $9,780, and deputy commissioner, $12,720. If my hon. friend has been taking these figures down I think he will find that they compare very favourably indeed with those of most police forces.
Can the minister tell me how many years men have to be with the service before they are permitted to marry? What are the latest regulations?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The general rule is five years. There are some limited exceptions at three years.

At this stage in the history of our country, Mr. Chairman, when married life is taken to be the normal way of life, and in view of the fact that the wife of the member of the R.C.M.P. invariably makes a useful contribution to the life of the community, I would think we should not argue that the economy of Canada cannot stand supporting an adequate R.C.M.P. force if the members of the force marry when they wish and whom they wish.
I recall that last year the minister said we accept about one out of 14 applicants. When we have such rigid tests I think it should be left to the good judgment of those who are selected to decide when they have found

a suitable girl to marry, and that the economy of Canada should be able to stand the provision of married quarters and an income that is adequate to enable members of the R.C.M.P. to assume the responsibilities of married life without waiting for five years or even for three years in the very exceptional cases that the minister referred to.
What study has been made of the matter, and what hope is there for a revision of the regulations in order to offer those who are accepted into the service the same privileges that other citizens of the country expect and demand?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think there are some in Canada who seem to be of the opinion that the rule of the force against marriage for the first five years is, as my hon. friend has indicated, a survival of medieval discipline that is imposed without relation to the normal needs and administration, of the force. But I can assure my hon. friend that that is by no means the case.
In the normal course of events about one year is required to train a new recruit to be a member of the force. During the next two years and to a lesser extent the two years following, in order for him to gain the experience he will require to discharge his duties as a member of the force-because, as I am sure the hon. member with his knowledge of Saskatchewan is aware, members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police are in small groups in places where they have quite a heavy responsibility-he will be moved an average of eight to ten times.
I do not need to tell the members of the committee that with the large number of isolated posts we have in the Arctic, and to an increasing extent since we have been building the D.E.W. line and so on, many of these places to which the younger men are posted are not places where they could take a wife and family with any degree of convenience at all. As a matter of fact it is quite a substantial problem just to see that the members of the forces are properly housed and fed. Therefore the purpose of the rule is to enable us to operate a force of the type of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in the kind of country in which we do operate, and to train the men properly during the first five-year period so they can have that degree of responsibility which we expect of them. Everyone who enters the force knows perfectly well when he does so that these are the rules of the game, and he is not in the force for any length of time before he becomes aware of the very good and substantial reasons that there are for these rules.
It is only in the exceptional case that the all too human failing comes into play, a failing

that I am sure we all share, and a member of the force happens to meet with some lady of such great charm that he cannot reconcile his undertaking to the force with the beauty of his fair one; and he gets married. He knows when he does that, he knows at every stage of the game, just what the consequences of his step will be.
It might be argued that we should not have this period of training. I do not know how we can expect to have trained people unless we train them; and unless we put them through that training. I do not know how we can expect to maintain the morale and the quality of the force so that the individual constable, wherever he may be, even if he is by himself, is a credit to the force. I certainly do not know how we could ever expect to provide facilities for women and babies in these northerly posts where, as I have said, it is an extremely difficult thing for us even to provide accommodation for the members of the force themselves.
This is by no means confined to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. The same problem is encountered by the northern contractors to whom reference was made earlier. If we are going to operate in that kind of country it is pretty difficult to operate in the same way that you would among the apartment houses of Ottawa.

Mr. Chairman, there are some questions on this item relating to discipline and similar matters that I think would properly be in order, but I do not want to anticipate a discussion that might well arise in connection with the legislation concerning the police which is to come before us later this session. I wanted to ask some questions and make some comments on disciplinary matters, but I will not do that now if I am correct in understanding that the legislation to come before us later will be bound to occasion a discussion of the code of discipline of the police force. May I have the minister's assurance on that point?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I want to be fair with my hon. friend. I do not think it will come in the amendments of this session. It will come in the general revision of the act when we get to it. If my hon. friend wishes to discuss that subject matter, I think perhaps it would be better for him to raise it at the present time.

Very well. I thank the minister for that explanation. Looking at the details on page 497 I notice that there has been an increase of virtually 320 in the strength of the force, land and air services, this year compared with last year. Preliminary to some comments and questions on
Supply-Justice
discipline, I should like to ask the minister if he will tell us what the situation is with regard to recruitment and whether the situation with respect to the urgent requirement for personnel-there was a considerable shortage-is now approaching the break-even point or whether there is still some urgency with respect to further recruiting.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think the general statement could be made that the present situation with regard to recruiting is not only very good but is also quite promising, and that we are working now toward providing the increased strength for which this item provides.

I guess I do not quite understand the minister. I understand there will be a strength of 3,995 regular members of the force and 455 special constables and employed civilians. I do not take it that that is an establishment. I take it that those are the actual numbers for whom it is necessary to provide pay for the fiscal year now under review. Would the minister say whether 1 am correct there, or is this an establishment which we have still to recruit in order to fill?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This particular estimate, like all of these estimates here, is the amount we think we shall need to spend in order to carry out the program which we have planned for ourselves in the ensuing fiscal year. In that sense it is an establishment within the meaning that my hon. friend I think is giving to the word. But it does not necessarily follow that we have at this instant the number that is outlined in this estimate.

There would always be variations from time to time within the year. If I can do so, I shall try to put it very shortly and simply. Are the 3,995 regular members of the force and 455 special constables and employed civilians the number which is deemed to be sufficient and adequate to meet the policing requirements of the force, or the duties of the force, during the fiscal year or do you still want more recruits to meet your present obligations?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The answer to that question is yes.
What is estimated now to be the approximate shortage in personnel?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You mean as of the present date?

All right; what is it as of the present date, or even when they have met what the minister says is what they anticipate they will require during the year? You just told me that is not enough, that it is not as
35S8

Supply-J ustice
many as you would like to have. By how much does it tall short of what you would like to have?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No. What I said is that we have not now as many as we would like to have, but that the present experience in recruiting is not only satisfactory but promising; and that we think we shall be able to recruit sufficient additional members to those we now have to meet the requirements for which we are seeking authority.
In other words, the numbers which I have already read out, and which I shall not repeat, it is anticipated will be filled this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

Now what I am asking is this. Is that number going to be sufficient? Are you going to be able to say, "We have now got what we need"? Or does this number represent only what you think you will be able to get and would it in fact be desirable if we had more police personnel on strength?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am sure my hon. friend realizes that neither the amount we have in fact nor the number we need is a static figure.
Exactly.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am sure he realizes that many of our needs we can foresee. Some of our needs we know we cannot foresee. Therefore as a practical matter we must review these figures from time to time; and some time this summer we will be reviewing these very figures that we are discussing. I do not know how I can make any more definite statement than I made when I said that we are in fairly good shape now; that the prospects are quite good; that we think we can recruit the additional numbers we require within what we can foresee at the present time; and that this summer we shall have to examine our position again in the usual manner in which we always do that.

I am sorry we cannot get closer together than that, but I will leave the matter. At any rate, there is to be an increase during this year over last year of some 400 members of the force, regular and special.
That raises the problem of discipline. The minister has mentioned the training which recruits are required to undergo. I know it is dangerous and unfair to draw general conclusions from individual cases, and I shall not do so. But one cannot help being concerned about the type of case I have in mind, namely the case which occurred in Prince George during 1955, which was a great discredit certainly to the individual members

of the force who took part in it and which I know was viewed with great seriousness by the senior officers of the force themselves. But even in the spirit of what I have said, namely that it is unfair to make too much of any one particular case, this was to such an extent the sort of thing we have always felt that the R.C.M.P. was above that by that very fact and, if you like, by the excellence of the record of the force over the years, it sticks out like a sore thumb.
I refer to the case of the two constables- fortunately it can be said that they were relatively junior-who beat a prisoner and extorted a confession from him, and who were found guilty of having done so. They were fined. They were reduced in rank. They were sentenced to imprisonment. One was sentenced to six months' imprisonment with hard labour and recommended for dismissal, and the other was sentenced to four months' imprisonment with hard labour and recommended for dismissal.
Both appealed as to sentence only, with the result that their fines were remitted. I do not suppose there is any point in imposing a fine which there is no opportunity to collect. It becomes senseless and only involves administrative red tape and does not produce any result. But I am surprised that this punishment-which I must say I find to be not by any means excessive in the light of the seriousness of the offence

was in any sense reduced on appeal.
I should like an explanation of that matter, because I personally was surprised. I was surprised because I felt the feeling would probably have been to make an example of these men. I do not think a fine-though it is admittedly only part of the sentence and there are other and perhaps more serious parts-in one case of $100 and in another of $60 is in any way excessive even though, as I said before, it is only part of a sentence.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sure none of the remarks which my hon. friend from Kamloops made with regard to the great embarrassment this incident caused the force, which has had a record from which this sort of thing is not ever expected, were in any way exaggerated. I am in complete agreement with him that this was a most regrettable episode in the history of the force.
As I understand my hon. friend's remarks with regard to the disposition of the cases of these two men, he does not disagree with the reduction in rank, with the imprisonment or with the dishonourable dismissal from the force, though he does think the remission of the fines was unwarranted. Well, that was ordered by the commissioner on the appeals which both these constables made to him. My

information is that the reason for the remission of the fines was that they were a relatively insignificant part of the total penalty. When a man is reduced in rank, imprisoned and kicked out of the force, it does not seem to me to make a great deal of difference whether or not he is fined a small amount such as $60.
Now, it may be that my hon. friend does not agree with that judgment, but it was one which the commissioner had the authority to make and which he did make, I am sure, with the same conscientious attitude toward his responsibilities that he shows on all occasions.

I do not believe we are going to quarrel over what would perhaps be properly regarded as an administrative detail in the exercise of the commissioner's discretion, except that I have just regretted, and we will leave it there, that the punishment was in any way lessened.
This occurs to me. While I am not sure that it would be in any sense a legal responsibility of the force, and in fact I am not quite clear how the matter would be handled, there does arise the question of making some measure of restitution to the individual who was wronged as a result of this offence. Is there anything that can be done along those lines, or was there any request made? If so, how was it made?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman, I understand that the man who was prejudiced by this conduct has made a claim for compensation which is under negotiation at the present time. When the negotiation is completed, I presume the matter will be taken care of by an ex gratia payment.

It was in that respect that it struck me that, small in total amount though the fines may be, nevertheless as a gesture or something that might be meaningful the fines might have been allowed to stand. However, I will not press it any further.
May I ask this. Everyone must recognize that an organization such as this, confronted with the twin difficulties of a quite rapid expansion and the necessity to maintain a high standard, has a very real problem. In asking this question I am not trying to cavil or overlook the fact that when you take on a large number of new men you do have these difficulties, but I should like to know whether any statistics are available, and if so what is their general effect, concerning the number of cases in which disciplinary action has had to be taken. Do the statistics show any trend which should be regarded seriously, or do they indicate an increase in that type of offence as a result of or accompanying the
Supply-Justice
rapid expansion of the force? How is the problem being dealt with?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I suppose what my hon. friend means is, is there any increase in the percentage of the total force represented by those who have committed offences of that type?
I do not mean small offences, but offences which would be regarded within the force itself as serious.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The commissioner tells me
that he has looked into this and that while he has no actual figures he has not been able to discern any noticeable or appreciable increase in offences of that character.

Mr. Chairman, on the point my hon. friend from Kamloops raised a moment ago about this fine and its remission, I quite agree with the minister that perhaps it was an insignificant part of the total penalty, and with the hon. member for Kamloops that there is no point in enlarging on it at this moment. However, I do think, as the minister said, it is something which is rather regrettable as far as the force is concerned. I think it is rather regrettable that there should have been any suggestion that it could be inferred that possibly this was condoned in some way. I know that was not the intention of the commissioner. I presume you are faced with constables who are in poor financial circumstances, and practically the same result was reached.
I know we are now approaching the hour of five o'clock, but when the item is up again -I presume it is not going to carry in the next few minutes-I should like the minister to be able to give us, for instance, the comparative figures on the strength of the force. We have the estimated strength for this year. What was the strength of the force say 10 years ago. I am somewhat concerned, because I have had something to do with this force in various ways, with the rapid increase and the fact that the junior men feel that perhaps they have to do things today to achieve a reputation and thereby obtain promotion which would be somewhat foreign to the officers and men of 10 or 20 years ago.
One does not want to be critical, but I just throw this out to the minister as a last word at this stage. I was talking to one of the superior court judges the other day, one whom I think the minister knows, and in speaking of the reputation of this force he said that if a senior officer came before him and gave evidence he would not have to be sworn; he would take his word. But if some of these junior fellows come before him and are sworn he still did not believe them because they were too anxious to get a conviction.

Public Works-Burrard Inlet, B.C.
Now, with these men coming into the force and belonging to something that is part of the fabric of Canadian tradition, I wonder if it is emphasized that although they have a responsibility for the enforcement of law, they have also a responsibility for maintaining the tradition of this force. If you have 10,000 where once you had 2,000, your chance of promotion may be lessened. There may be a tendency to think that if you get a lot of convictions, get enough scalps hanging from your belt, you will get promotion quicker. I think that is the view of some of the juniors with whom I have spoken. They seemed to express that view.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In order that the question which my hon. friend has raised might have the reply right next to it in Hansard, might I say that on March 31, 1946, the 10 years ago to which my hon. friend referred, the force had in uniform 2,526 men; special constables, 460; civilians, 212; civil servants, 441, or a total of 3,639. On April 28, 1956, the force had in uniform 4,604; special constables, 347; civilians, 495; civil servants, 912, or a total of 6,358. As my hon. friend knows, the ambit of the responsibilities of the force during that 10-year period has been greatly widened. We have a number of new contracts with provinces; we have a special division, and we have a heavier problem of security. Unless these differences in responsibility are taken into account it would not be fair to base any kind of judgment upon the difference between the 3,639 figure in 1946 and the 6,358 figure for 1956.

I was not criticizing the increase in the force. I was just suggesting the difficulty in obtaining promotion because there ,was so much competition.

Bill No. 230 is a rather unusual case. The petitioner in this instance comes from British Columbia. She reported that she had been married some 24 years ago, in 1932. This woman was a particularly good witness. She was asked the following question:
Will you tell the committee what you think broke up this marriage? You seemed to get along all right until the forties.
Her answer was:
I think it was just bad luck, and the war separated us. Six years of separation is a long time. That is just about as near as 1 can make any comment on it.
The conclusion was, of course, that this was another war tragedy. The witness was given very sympathetic consideration by Their Honours the senators. Senator Smith asked:
Why is it that you come to us with this petition? Why have you not gone through this proceeding in the ordinary course down in British Columbia?
The answer was:
I cannot get a divorce out there, with my husband domiciled in Montreal.
This brings me to one point, Mr. Chairman. I think equality of the sexes should be established as far as granting divorce is concerned. These people were married in British Columbia; they spent none of their married life in the province of Quebec. As I recall the evidence they were both in Great Britain and Europe for part of their married life; but because the husband now happens to be living in the province of Quebec this unfortunate woman is placed in the position where she must come all the way from British Columbia to Ottawa to have her case presented and the divorce granted. It would seem to me that because this woman was domiciled in British Columbia with her husband for most of their married life, because she married, lived and made a living there, she should not now be obliged to come to Ottawa to place her grievance before us.
In Bill No. 233 we have a development which is occurring more frequently and which is going to eliminate the expense in connection with detectives to a large extent. In this case both the petitioner and the respondent appeared. In Bill No. 234 the respondent and the co-respondent came along. In Bill No. 240 the people concerned managed without any paid detectives.
In the case of Bill No. 243 I find that the evidence was supplied by two members of

In the case of Bill No. 244 the respondent appeared. It would seem that if the respondent is ready to admit the charges which are made, that evidence is accepted. It takes a great deal less time than to hear evidence given by paid detectives.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING BRITISH COLUMBIA PUBLIC CARRIERS BY WATER UNDER JURISDICTION OF TRANSPORT COMMISSION
AMENDMENT TO BRING BRITISH COLUMBIA PUBLIC CARRIERS BY WATER UNDER JURISDICTION OF TRANSPORT COMMISSION
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 107, to amend the Transport Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I should like to remind the house that the subject matter of this bill is not new as far as discussion by myself is concerned. When the first item of the estimates of the Minister of Transport was under discussion last year I spoke at some length and outlined the problem that exists, in my view, in respect to coastal transportation by water in British Columbia. I pointed out that it appeared to me that this particular form of transportation was almost the only type of transportation in Canada without any proper form of regulation by a public authority.
I do not intend to repeat the remarks I made last year, or for that matter the year before, when the transport estimates were under discussion because they are to be found in Hansard of July 20, 1955, at page 6474 and the pages following. However, I should like simply to point out that on that occasion
Transport Act
I did mention several examples of the situation in which people had been finding themselves on the coast of British Columbia because in respect to services that are maintained or not maintained, in respect to the rates that are charged or the changes that are made from time to time in those rates. I mentioned as one example how one of the transportation companies had without any prior notice to its patrons increased its rates by 33J per cent. They had discovered it only through invoices which they received later from the firms from which they had purchased goods.
So I thought the time had come when this particular problem should be brought to the attention of the house in the form of a bill to amend the Transport Act to meet, in some measure at least, the situation that exists. The bill itself is a very simple one. It simply removes from the act a part which deletes from the general provisions that are in the act for the regulation of transportation by water, ports or places in the province of British Columbia.
The situation I described last year continues, and the problem affects not only areas I mentioned last year but areas I did not mention at that time. As a further example of the need for some proper action to bring coastal transportation under regulation, I wish to draw your attention in particular at this time to the situation on the west coast of Vancouver island. There a service is in operation by the Canadian Pacific Steamship Company, and has been in operation by that company for a long period of time. In years gone by the service was carried on by a very well known vessel, the S.S. Princess Maquinna, which had become quite a tradition on the coast of British Columbia. Over quite a number of years that service was in receipt of a subsidy from the federal government. But at the present time the service is carried on by quite a small vessel known as the Princess of Alberni, and no subsidy is being paid.
I might interpolate here that at the present time the only segment of the coastal transport system in British Columbia that does come under any form of government regulation, as far as I am aware, is one of the services operated by Union Steamships, which does receive a subvention from the federal government for the operation of that service and, therefore, is subject to some jurisdiction by the Canadian maritime commission.
In my considered opinion the service being operated at this time on the west coast of Vancouver island is a disgrace to the name of the Canadian Pacific Railway. In fact I would go so far as to suggest that if the

Transport Act
president of the Canadian Pacific Railway-Company has any doubts as to the correctness of the statements I have made, he might very well try going out to the Pacific coast incognito and spending two or three months in one of the west coast logging camps. There I am sure he would come to realize, if he had to live in an isolated community depending entirely, as far as supplies were concerned, on the service which is being operated under the banner of his company, that something should be done about that situation.
I have a communication here that is in the form of a petition from one of these west coast communities to which I have referred. I am going to read a short excerpt from their remarks to illustrate my point. This was signed by practically everyone in this community. I shall not read the entire petition, but it says:
At present we rely solely on the C.P.R. for delivery of groceries, mail and bulk supplies. To say the least, this service is not adequate, e.g. "on December 9 the C.P.R. failed to deliver 11 bags of mail and when asked for this mail the crew replied that it wasn't on board. Later at Zeballos, on this same trip, the Gold River mail was discovered and was then carried back to Vancouver and then to Gold River on December 19, thus making it impossible for residents to send out Christmas parcels on time.
In addition, there are numerous instances of essential supplies not being delivered.
That is merely one example. I am sure that if only 10 per cent of the complaints that have come to my ears in respect to the kind of service presently being offered by the C.P.R. are well founded, the statement contained in this petition is more than borne out. I have heard of a situation arising when people were expecting a new chesterfield, and it happened for some reason or other to be dropped into the salt water and that was the end of it as far as the people were concerned. I have heard of shipments having been made and receipts having been given for them by the sender, but they were never received by the consignee. Apparently there is no recourse whatever in respect to this kind of situation.
Quite frankly I have not found the attitude taken by the officials of this company on the west coast to have been very co-operative. I have had the experience of approaching them and getting the impression that as far as I was concerned as the member representing the people of that constituency in this house, the kind of service that was given was just none of my business. I like to feel that I am prepared to listen to both sides of a question, but certainly my experience in this instance, when I was willing to hear the side of the company, was that I was simply given a rather quick brush-off.
Together with previous statements I have made, Mr. Speaker, that is an outline of some

of the reasons why I feel that I should bring this question to the attention of the house at this time in the form of a bill calling for an amendment to the Transport Act to provide some form of court of appeal for the people who are dependent upon coastal transportation services for all their supplies and transportation.
During the course of looking into the matter I took it upon myself to try to find out something of the background of the present Transport Act, and I discovered that the original act was introduced in the Senate in the year 1937 and was discussed by a committee of that house at that time, but that no action was taken on it in this house that year. However, in the year 1938 a rather modified bill was introduced in this house by the then minister of transport, now Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). I find that some of the remarks he made on moving second reading of the bill are to me at least of considerable interest today. As found on page 1554 of Hansard for March 21, 1938, he had this to say in introducing the bill:
Mr. Speaker, the object of this hill is to promote the stabilization of the transport industry in Canada, in the public interest as well as in the interests of all those engaged in transportation.
Later, as found on the same page, he said:
It is a matter of public interest that transportation rates be reasonably stable, and applied without discrimination. Experience has shown that publicity is essential to prevent discrimination. Therefore the publicity of rates is a fundamental requirement in this bill.
We also appreciate that our transportation rate structure may break down completely unless some relation is maintained between transportation charges and the abilities of various commodities to stand those charges. There is also the problem of conditions of employment in transportation industries. It will not be a question that it is the duty and interest of all employers to endeavour to maintain reasonable standards of conditions and rewards of employment. The absence of regulation and the resulting uneconomical competition must inevitably bear heavily on the workers, since labour costs comprise such a large proportion of operating expenses. The wide difference in working conditions, as between regulated transportation and unregulated transportation, must be apparent to all. Apart from the effect on labour, the interest of public safety is also involved.
Objections to this bill have taken the form, not that regulation is undesirable, but rather that the means provided by the bill may work hardship in certain specific instances. Many have objected on the ground that the bill will have the effect of increasing rates. I see nothing in the bill which can reasonably lead to that conclusion. The fact is that Canadian railway rates, as established under regulation, are among the lowest in the world, and this has been accomplished notwithstanding the fact that Canada is a sparsely populated country. Regulation should have the effect of lowering rather than raising rates, by tending to eliminate wasteful and destructive competition among the various forms of transportation.

I think some of the statements made in 1938 by the then minister of transport hold equally good today and are applicable to the situation prevailing at the present time in the coastal areas of British Columbia. In looking at the debates of that time, Mr. Speaker, I was also interested to discover that the then member for Comox-Alberni, Mr. A. W. Neill, who represented that constituency in the house from 1921 to 1945, was also very much concerned with this problem. I may say I was also very much interested to discover that the conclusion Mr. Neill came to in 1938, after having had a good many years of experience in the house, was identical with the conclusion I have come to after having given some attention to the problem since I have been the member for that constituency.
Mr. Neill's remarks when speaking on second reading of the bill can be found at page 1560 of Hansard for March 21, 1938. He had been referring to some other sections of the bill, and then had this to say:
. . . but the part that I have more interest in is the next:
"5. The provisions of this part shall not apply in the case of ships engaged in the transport of goods or passengers
(a) between ports or places in British Columbia."
As far as we in British Columbia are concerned, that of course entirely annihilates the whole purpose of the bill.
In fact, Mr. Neill was so convinced of the correctness of that position that when the bill was being considered in committee he moved for the deletion of the particular section of the bill which my bill now proposes to delete from the act, that is, the exempting provision in respect of ports or places in British Columbia. Even at that time this was not a new matter as far as Mr. Neill was concerned, and although he was not a member of the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines he took the trouble to appear as a witness before the committee when it was considering the bill. In his statement, as recorded on page 113 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines of 1938, Mr. Neill had this to say:
Bill B of the Senate of last year, on which the present bill is largely founded, when first introduced contained no such provision excluding the coastal waters, but it was amended to that effect, apparently, by the standing committee of the Senate . . .
A little later he had this to say:
I submit that it is highly desirable that such control should be exercised. The need for it is so apparent, in British Columbia at least, that in 1935 I introduced a bill to amend the Railway Act to that effect, which bill was defeated in the House of Commons. The debate will be found in Hansard of February 12, 1935, and later on in Hansard of February 22. There is a precedent of
Transport Act
long standing for this provision because some 30 years ago the then section 7 of the Railway Act provided that the Railway Act should apply to traffic carried by sea or inland waters between any ports or places in Canada. There was, however, a provision attached to it that it only applied to boats owned or chartered by a railway company.
I was interested in looking back in the record to discover just what that bill which Mr. Neill introduced at that time-that is in 1935-was all about. I discovered that in the course of debate on his bill, in which Mr. Manion, the then minister of railways, participated, it was brought out that while even at that time there had been in the Railway Act for 30 years a section calling for some exercise of control by the board of railway commissioners over water transportation carried on by a railway company, that section had never been put into effect.
As I understand it, that section is still to be found in the Railway Act and is section 363 of the present act. In order to be sure on this point I had a question on the order paper earlier this year which was answered on February 23. I asked whether this section had ever been applied. The answer I received was no. It is therefore apparent that neither as to ships operated by railway companies nor as to ships operated by independent shipping companies is there any form of public control over their operations, as to whether or not they maintain schedules, whether or not they stop giving service to the communities, or as to the question of the rates they may charge from time to time.
The purpose of Mr. Neill's bill back in 1935 was to broaden the application of that section of the Railway Act to include ships which were operated by companies other than railway companies. It was in the course of that debate that it was brought out that the section had never come into operation.
I realize that this whole question of transportation is an extremely complicated matter. I am putting this proposition forward in this amending bill in the hope that the situation which I have attempted to describe may be corrected. In a matter as complicated as this I realize that there may be aspects of the matter which have not occurred to me. To me this is the kind of bill which should be considered in a committee of the house where those concerned, such as transport companies and others, would have the opportunity of making representations. I say this in order to make it perfectly clear that if this bill is successful in passing second reading, as far as I am concerned I should be happy to have it considered by a committee of the house.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING BRITISH COLUMBIA PUBLIC CARRIERS BY WATER UNDER JURISDICTION OF TRANSPORT COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the house feels indebted to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) for having raised this important subject. It is one of considerable complexity, and any change will affect the economy of all those people who live in the scattered communities of the west coast. When I say that we are indebted to the hon. member for having raised the problem, I do not want it to be construed that I am in favour of this bill.
I refer only to the importance of the problem. The problem is so important that the royal commission on shipping was given special instructions to inquire into conditions on the west coast of British Columbia.
It is well to get a picture of the types of communities involved and the conditions under which many of them live. Of course we have the great metropolitan area of Vancouver on the mainland. Then there are other cities such as Victoria and Prince Rupert. But along that very indented coastline there are innumerable villages and logging and mining camps, the vast majority of which are dependent upon sea communication for the bringing in of the supplies they need. At least they have been dependent upon sea communications until very recent years. I submit that considerable changes have taken place since this matter was previously discussed in the house in Mr. Neill's time.
In order to give some idea of the kind of shipping and the variety of types of vessels which serve these communities, I should like to give some statistics. From such research as I have been able to carry out I find that there are 54 passenger and freight vessels of a gross tonnage of over 80 tons operating on regular schedules on this coast. That is only one form of shipping. In addition to that, there are some 29 special purpose covered barges of 23,250 deadweight tons and some 310 open scows of 163,200 deadweight tons. They range from 350 tons to 2,000 tons per vessel. There are also some 781 open barges, and 52 towboat companies whose fleet numbers 315 towboats ranging from 100 horsepower to 2,600 horsepower.
That information gives you some idea of the vast amount of shipping there is on the west coast. It also gives you an idea of the range of types of vessels, from tugboats and scows to big steamships, carrying a great quantity of cargo. During 1954-that is the last year for which I obtained any figures-1,209 deep sea vessels entered British Columbia ports. These vessels brought into British Columbia 1,697,168 tons of cargo and exported over 6 million tons. To give some idea of the passenger traffic that is going on, I would point out that during last year in the harbours of Sidney

and Victoria combined, 89,398 cars were handled through customs and the number of passengers handled by the customs in Sidney and Victoria combined amounted to 265,915. I think those figures will give some idea of the volume of shipping and the amount of cargo that must be moved.
There is a considerable difference in the way the steamship companies estimate their charges and the way in which the tugboats estimate their charges and rates for carrying freight. The tugboats sometimes have a flat rate from point to point; sometimes a flat rate within a certain zone, but more usually they quote a daily rate and that depends very largely on the length of the tow and the weather conditions.
Now, the towboat industry has developed greatly during the last five years. The steamship companies are facing very serious competition from these towboat companies. Actually some of the runs which previously were profitable for the steamship companies through the gulf islands and up the west coast of Vancouver island are no longer profitable and the companies are faced with the choice of either reducing their services or operating at a loss.
From the steamship point of view, therefore, the officials of these companies feel that they must have freedom of action in making quotations if they are to maintain the traffic level which exists now. They must also be able to make competitive quotations at very short notice, and any attempt to regulate those quotations made by steamship companies in order to compete with towboat companies would present almost insurmountable difficulties.
Then, in addition to the freight and passenger traffic carried by water a new element has entered into the problem, and that is the large number of passengers and freight now carried by the air lines. A lot of freight is carried not only by T.C.A. but the other air line companies operating on the west coast. There is a continual stream of passengers being carried by the air lines. In considering the whole situation, it would be unfair to regulate the rates being charged for freight and passengers on vessels and not impose similar regulations to affect the movement of passengers and freight by air.
It seems to me that if this bill to amend the Transport Act carries, we have to go very much further than is indicated by the bill at the present time. Even if it applied to goods and passengers moving between ports and places on the west coast the smaller vessels would be excluded, and that would mean that many of the towboats, scows,

barges, etc. would be able to operate without any limitation. It should, therefore, not only apply to vessels which are over 100 tons but must be made applicable to this great fleet of smaller craft. If it were made applicable to the smaller craft, then I think it would be impractical to enforce. It must also be applied to passengers and freight being carried by air.
In addition we must remember that Canadian lines and Canadian merchants are in very active competition with the steamship lines and tugboat services from United States ports such as Seattle and elsewhere along the Washington and Oregon coasts. We have vessels from the United States plying between United States ports through Canadian waters to Alaska, and in some cases stopping off at various points along the Canadian coast. I am inclined to think that the competition at present is sufficient to assure equality without introducing further regulations.
I have endeavoured to find out what some of the organizations in my own constituency felt about this matter. I communicated with a number of organizations, some interested and some not biased in any way. I shall not quote what the steamship and tugboat companies have to say, but I think it is interesting to hear the opinion of the chambers of commerce of a couple of small communities.
We are most emphatically opposed to the amendment. We believe that to bring the public carriers by water under the jurisdiction of the board of transport commissioners would greatly hamper our commerce and progress.

I have another expression of opinion from the Sooke-Jordan River chamber of commerce, and I am particularly mentioning the small places. They feel opposed to the proposed legislation outlined as they think it would be detrimental to free enterprise.

Questions

Guysborough):
1.	Is the federal government participating financially with the government of the province of Nova Scotia in a forest inventory survey in Nova Scotia?
2.	If so. what is the basis for sharing costs?
3.	How much money did the federal government contribute in the past fiscal year, and how much to date?
4.	Is the inventory completed?
5.	If not, when will it be completed?
Answer by: Hon. Jean Lesage (Minister of
Northern Affairs and National Resources):
1.	Yes.
2.	The basis for sharing the costs is a payment of 50 per cent by the federal government and 50 per cent by the province.
3.	The federal government contributed $121,616 in the fiscal year 1955-56 and a total of $234,261 to date.
4.	No.
5.	It is expected that the inventory will be completed by March 31, 1957, with continuing work after that time being devoted to, keeping the inventory up to date.
